title: Roast Gravy
subtitle: Rich pan gravy from roasting juices
excerpt: A proper roast gravy made from the caramelised roasting pan juices, deglazed with wine and thickened with flour. The definitive accompaniment to any British roast.

recipe.sourceNotes: Gravy is the defining sauce of British cooking. At its simplest it is just the pan juices from roasting diluted with water; at its best it is built from carefully caramelised meat drippings, deglazed with wine, and enriched with good stock. The word 'gravy' comes from the medieval French 'grané', referring to the cooking juices of meat. The key difference between a good gravy and a mediocre one is the fond: the dark, sticky, caramelised bits stuck to the bottom of the roasting pan after the meat has rested. This is where the flavour is concentrated. Scraping it up with liquid and incorporating it into the gravy base is what gives real depth. This recipe is a method that applies to any roast, using the pan drippings as the fat for the roux.

recipeTools.notes: The tin used to roast the meat.

content.text: The fat from the drippings is the base for the roux. Pour off the fat from the resting meat and measure it: you need about 2 tablespoons. Tip it back into the roasting tin. The dark bits stuck to the bottom are the fond, and scraping them up with the wine is what gives real flavour. Good stock is essential here: thin, pale stock produces thin, pale gravy.
Pour off the fat from the roasting tin, leaving the juices and the caramelised fond. Set the tin over medium heat on the hob. Add 2 tablespoons of the reserved fat back in.
Scatter the flour over the fat and stir into the pan juices. Cook for 2 minutes, scraping up all the dark bits from the bottom. The mixture will look dark and dry.
Pour in the wine. Stir vigorously, scraping up any remaining fond. Let it bubble for 1 minute.

Add the stock gradually, whisking to prevent lumps. Bring to a simmer and cook for 8 to 10 minutes, stirring frequently, until thickened to a coating consistency. Add the Worcestershire sauce. Season with salt and pepper. Strain through a fine sieve into a jug if you prefer a smooth gravy. Serve immediately.
